newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Fourteen die in Pakistan sectarian, ethnic attacks.
newsitem.headline: Fourteen die in Pakistan sectarian, ethnic attacks.

text.p: At least 14 people were killed in a wave of Moslem sectarian and ethnic attacks in Pakistan on Wednesday and Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif hinted of possible intervention in the provinces to maintain law and order.

At least 10 people were killed and more than 30 wounded in gun and bomb attacks in populous Punjab province in the latest incidents in a wave of violence between rival militant groups of the majority Sunni and the minority Shi'ite Moslem sects, police and witnesses said.
At least four people were killed in what appeared to be ethnic violence Karachi, Pakistan's commercial hub, police there said.

Sharif discussed the law and order situation with his cabinet at a meeting in Islamabad and asked the Interior Ministry to set up round-the-clock control room to monitor the situation in the provinces, a government statement said.

It quoted him as telling the cabinet that, "while he had the greatest respect for the autonomy of the provinces as provided under the constitution, the federal government could not remain indefinitely indifferent to the situation".
The remark appeared to be warning to the provinces that the federal government could intervene if they failed to check the new upsurge of violence.

Gunmen attacked a Sunni sect mosque in Punjab capital Lahore at the end of evening prayers, killing at six people and injuring two, hours after a Shi'ite sect follower was shot dead in a city bazaar, the police said.
A bomb hurled at a night prayer meeting at a Sunni mosque in the main southern Punjab city of Multan killed three men and injured about 30, witnesses and doctors said.
There was no immediate information about the identity of the attackers, who struck after 12 people, most of them Shi'ites, were killed in three shootouts in Punjab on Monday.

Sectarian violence is rife in Punjab with militant Sunni and Shi'ite factions engaged in a feud that officials say has killed more than 130 people so far this year, including religious scholars, lawyers and doctors.
Lawyers in Lahore boycotted courts on Wednesday to protest at the killings of their colleagues in sectarian violence.
Supreme Court Chief Justice Sajjad Ali Shah set Saturday for a hearing he is planning in Lahore to try to determine the causes of the violence.
Sunni groups accuse neighbouring Shi'ite Iran of financing Pakistani Shi'ite militants, while Shi'ites accuse Sunni Saudi Arabia of aiding Sunni groups.

Sunni-Shi'ite disputes over Islamic beliefs have often spilled into violence in Pakistan. Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's mainly Sunni population of more than 135 million but are the majority in Iran.

In Karachi, gunmen entered a house in the Saudabad district and shot dead a brother and cousin of a journalist working for the local media. In separate incidents, an unidentified body stuffed into a sack was found in the Liaquatabad area and a man was killed by gunfire in Shah Latif Town, police said.
They had no word on the motives for the killings, the latest in a surge of violence in Karachi in recent weeks.
Militants of Mutahida National Movement, which was until last month known as the Mohajir National Movement (MQM), have been feuding with supporters of the breakaway Haqiqi group.
More than 225 people have died in ethnic, sectarian and political violence in Karachi this year, compared to about 500 last year and more than 2,000 in 1995.
